hero.name: Spiros Leividiotis
hero.subtitle: Staff Product Motion Designer specializing in motion systems and design system implementation. I help teams ship motion that's consistent, scalable, and implementation ready, turning principles into patterns, guidelines, and Lottie ready handoff with design systems and engineering.

bio: I'm Spiros, a Staff Product Motion Designer based in Amsterdam, working at the intersection of product design, animation, and design systems. I use motion as a functional tool to clarify interactions, reinforce hierarchy, and improve usability at scale.

Currently at Qonto, I built the motion design system from scratch and collaborate closely with product designers, design systems leads, and engineers. I focus on building reusable, well-documented motion patterns that teams can confidently use across complex products from Rive prototypes and Lottie pipelines to motion tokens and implementation specs.

Outside of work, I spend a lot of time cycling and hanging out with Finn, my westie - who has strong opinions about walk schedules and absolutely none about motion design. I care deeply about craft, consistency, and pragmatism, and I believe great motion should feel invisible: intentional, purposeful, and grounded in real user needs.

projects.name: Motion Design System
projects.bodyHtml:
2025 - 2026 Staff Motion Designer, Design System
Motion Design Design System Documentation Platform

Built a scalable motion language that bridges design and engineering—principles, patterns, tokens, documentation.

Context

The Problem

Qonto's design system provided clarity for color, typography, spacing, and components. But motion? It was inconsistent. Designers mocked up animations with arbitrary values. Engineers implemented them differently across platforms. There was no shared vocabulary.

We needed a motion system that would scale—one that designers could reference in specs, engineers could implement without ambiguity, and teams could extend without breaking consistency.

Goals & scope

Why motion, and what we aimed for

Motion is more than decoration. It creates clarity, focus, and flow—helping users understand what’s changing, navigate interfaces more easily, and feel connected to the product. Without a consistent system, we risk cluttered UIs, confusing transitions, and a product that feels slow and static instead of alive and responsive.

Our goals: a scalable, consistent motion design system that improves UX through predictable interactions; bakes motion into components; aligns design and dev handoff with shared tokens and specs; keeps web, iOS, and Android in sync; and empowers designers to design with motion from day one.

The solution rested on three pillars: Foundations (core properties, tokens, motion types and styles), Documentation & handoff (design-system section, linked specs, naming, training), and Integration—embedding motion in components and defining high-impact use cases (state change, visibility, screen transitions, content change) and shared patterns (cards, lists, modals).

Approach

Building the System

01 Motion Principles

We started by defining motion principles—the foundation for every animation decision. These principles guide what good motion feels like at Qonto: purposeful, coherent, subtle, snappy, and smooth.

Each principle came with visual examples showing do's and don'ts, helping teams understand not just the rules, but the reasoning behind them.

02 Primitives: Speaking the Same Language

Next, we worked with engineers to define primitive tokens—the building blocks of motion. We asked them what they needed: duration values, easing curves, scale factors, blur intensities.

We talked to designers about how they spec'd motion in mockups. The result: a shared vocabulary. motion.duration.quick means 200ms everywhere—Figma, iOS, Android, Web. No interpretation. No ambiguity.

Primitives include: Duration, Easing, Scale, Alpha, Blur, Translate, Delay, and Spring.

03 Semantics: Scalable Behaviors

Primitives alone weren't enough. Designers don't think in milliseconds and cubic-beziers—they think in behaviors. "This button should feel responsive." "This modal should slide in smoothly."

So we created semantic tokens—predefined combinations of primitives for common patterns. Behaviors like Fade, Slide, Press/Tap, Hover/Lift, and Expand/Collapse.

These semantics are organized into Base (entry, exit, reveal, transition) and Common (interactions, micro-animations). They're documented with specs, code snippets, and live previews.

Base Patterns

Entry
Exit
Reveal
Transition

Common Interactions

Press/Tap
Hover/Lift
Expand/Collapse
Slide
Scale Fade
Shimmer Loading
Stagger
Page Transition
Impact

The Result

Implementation with the motion system is faster. Designers know what behaviors to use from the library. Engineers reference tokens in code—no guesswork, no back-and-forth.

We scale. New features ship with consistent motion because the patterns are already defined. We're consistent across web and mobile because we share the same source of truth.

Most importantly, we have a common motion language. Designers, engineers, and product teams can discuss animation with precision, using the same vocabulary.

projects.bodyHtml:
Animation Production Lottie Technical Pipeline

I led the management of a 1,000+ Lottie animation library at Qonto—producing animations, leading the JSON → .lottie migration, and managing the technical pipeline across teams.

2022 - 2026 Staff Motion Designer, Design System
TLDR

1,000+ Lottie library. JSON → .lottie migration. Technical owner.

Managed 1,000+ Lottie library across product, website, marketing. Produced animations, led 6-month JSON → .lottie migration, and became technical owner for format guidelines and cross-platform compatibility.

1,000+
Lottie Files
3
Platforms
JSON → .lottie
Format Migration
Production

Managing at Scale

I managed a 1,000+ Lottie animation library across Qonto's product, website, and marketing. Produced animations alongside other motion designers, optimized for performance, and ensured consistency across platforms.

Built the pipeline: LottieFiles library structure, export standards, and led JSON → .lottie migration with engineers over 6 months—reducing file sizes, improving Android performance. Became technical owner for format guidelines and cross-platform troubleshooting.

Documentation

Lottie Center

Lottie Center is the internal hub I created so designers and stakeholders have one place for standards and how‑to’s: step-by-step guides (create, export, naming, delivery), technical specs, and handoff paths for in-app vs website.

Standards I documented:

  • Size: up to 500kb
  • Frame rate: 25fps or 30fps
  • Format: .json for web, .lottie for Android, iOS and Web

Documented flows: create & export, naming (in-app vs website), delivery to product and web, LottieFiles workflow, and sharing with internal and external partners.

Library

Selected Work

Impact

Beyond Individual Files

The library became a shared production asset across teams. Engineers integrated confidently. Designers referenced existing work. The .lottie migration improved Android performance across the entire product.

Motion Design Rive Product Thinking Implementation QA

Motion specs bridge design intent and user experience. I prototype in Rive, apply system tokens, create detailed specs, and QA on real devices. Each spec challenges: why this timing? why this easing? what's the user feeling?

2022 - 2026 Staff Motion Designer, Design System
TLDR

Rive prototypes → production specs. Challenging UX thinking.

Real product specs with custom timing curves, stagger patterns, and choreographed sequences. Implementation-ready, production-tested.

Loading state for card switching: existing card fades out to 40% → spinner fades in and out → new card fades in with shine effect. Spinner on card only (best for short load times, already used on platform). Spec uses motion tokens throughout.

projects.name: Brand Guidelines
projects.bodyHtml:
Flink, a fast-growing grocery delivery startup, needed motion design for their core brand touchpoints—logo animation, app endscreen, and splashscreen. The brief: create animations that communicated speed, reliability, and energy while maintaining technical feasibility for fast-paced product development.

2021 - 2022 Senior Motion Designer
Context

The Challenge

Flink's brand promise was fast delivery—groceries in minutes. The motion design had to reflect that: snappy, energetic, immediate. But it also had to work at scale: lightweight files, performant animations, and designs that wouldn't slow down app load times.

I focused on three key deliverables: a logo animation for brand moments, an app endscreen for post-order confirmation, and a splashscreen for app launch—each serving a specific user need and brand moment.

Deliverables

Core Brand Animations

Logo Animation

A quick, energetic reveal for brand moments—ads, presentations, app launches. The animation reinforces Flink's speed and energy without overstaying its welcome.

Overview

Endscreen for Ads & Video

A versatile end card for commercials, YouTube videos, social content, and other video formats. Reinforces the brand at the close of any spot.

App Splashscreen

An optimized launch animation that loads instantly and feels fast—even during network delays. Reinforces brand identity without creating perceived slowness.

Alternative

Explorations

Design Approach

Fast, Light, Energetic

Every animation was designed with speed as a constraint. I kept timings tight—most animations under 1 second. File sizes were optimized (Lottie exports under 30KB). Colors and shapes were simplified for performance.

The motion language was consistent: sharp, confident movements with quick easings. Nothing felt sluggish or over-animated. The brand moved like it delivered—fast, precise, and reliable.

These weren't just brand decorations—they were functional touchpoints that reinforced Flink's value proposition at key moments in the user journey.

Impact

Motion as Brand Identity

These animations became part of Flink's brand toolkit—used across the app, marketing materials, and internal presentations. They gave the brand a consistent motion personality: energetic, fast, and confident.

More importantly, they demonstrated how motion design can work within tight constraints—startup timelines, performance budgets, and rapid iteration cycles—while still delivering polished, on-brand results.
